title: An Indictment: Whose Responsibility for the Failure of 1942
byline: by Ram Swarup · Changers' Publications, pamphlet no. 1 · c. 1946
lede: An early polemic by Ram Swarup, written after the Congress leaders were released from prison at the end of the war. His starting point: a world war had transformed other countries yet left India “the same masters” and “the same leaders”. The people did their part in August 1942. The movement failed, he argues, because of the leadership. He says they treated the war as a moral question, adopted the Allies' framing, never planned or trained for a revolt, and afterwards called the people who did the fighting “mobs”.
facts: short sections, ending in a formal indictment
Britain declares war; Gandhi says India should not bargain
the Allahabad meeting, which he describes as discussing the demand as if it had already been granted
the Quit India resolution and “Do or Die”
note: This is a short wartime pamphlet with a deliberately harsh tone; its editor says as much. Historians weigh the 1942 movement differently: as a failure in the short term, and as a turning point that showed Britain it could not hold India much longer. This page summarises Ram Swarup's argument, attributed to him.

sections.eyebrow: Sections 3 and 6 · the record he cites
sections.title: From the outbreak of war to August 1942
items: Viceroy Linlithgow invites India to play its part. Gandhi advises support “unconditionally”.
Condemns fascism and asks Britain to state its war aims for India.
Peace needs democracy extended to “all colonial countries”.
The war is “essentially a moral issue”, not a chance to bargain.
Gandhi's draft says the British should “clear out”. Nehru and Azad object.
Quit India, while still aiming to help the Allied cause.
Students, workers and peasants act alone; the leaders are in prison.
Leaders disown the violence or claim credit, and no inquiry is held.

sections.title: What the leaders did, and what he says they should have done

cols.k: What they did, in his account
items: Accepted the Allies' “fascism versus democracy” framing
Nehru refused to meet Mussolini over Ethiopia
“We hate imperialism but we hate fascism more”
See the crisis as an opportunity
Put Indian freedom first, with “undivided loyalty”
Stop Indian troops being used to suppress other colonies

sections.eyebrow: Sections 6–8 · the conduct of the revolt
sections.title: Why the revolt failed, in his view
items: Leaders debated the demand as if Britain would agree, then worried about the consequences.
Pant: no disagreement on non-violence, only “about its effectiveness”.
Without training, he says, “Do or Die” meant dying, not doing.
Talk of victory within a week left people unready for a long struggle.

sections.title: Four counts against the leadership
items: They relied on moral slogans instead of seeing how events connected.
They made speeches instead of planning and training for the struggle.
They set up no inquiry into why the movement failed.
They belittled people like Subhas Bose and Jayaprakash Narayan, who saw what was at stake.
